q: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) is based on the conservation of:
explanation: KCL: the algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero, because charge cannot accumulate at a node — conservation of charge.
why: Energy conservation is the basis of KVL, not KCL.
Momentum has no role in circuit laws.
Flux conservation relates to magnetic circuits, not KCL.

q: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) is a consequence of the conservation of:
explanation: Around any closed loop the sum of voltage rises equals the sum of drops: net energy gained by a charge going round a loop is zero.
why: Power factor is not a conserved quantity.
Current is not a conserved quantity in this sense.

q: Thevenin's equivalent of a linear two-terminal network is:
options: A current source in parallel with a resistance
A voltage source in series with an impedance
A voltage source in parallel with an impedance
A current source in series with an impedance
explanation: Thevenin: Vth (open-circuit voltage) in series with Zth (impedance seen at the terminals with independent sources killed).
why: A voltage source in parallel with an element fixes the terminal voltage — not an equivalent of a general network.
A current source in series makes the series element irrelevant.

q: Norton's current I_{N} is the:
options: Current through the Thevenin resistance with load open
Open-circuit voltage divided by load resistance
explanation: I_{N} is found by shorting the output terminals: I_{N} = I_{sc} = V_{th}/R_{th}.
why: Load current depends on R_{L}; I_{N} does not.
With the load open no current flows in R_{th} of the Thevenin model.
Load resistance plays no part in finding I_{N}.

q: A network has V_{th} = 12 V and R_{th} = 4 Ω. Current in a 2 Ω load connected across it is:
explanation: I = 2 A

q: Maximum power is transferred from a DC source to a load when the load resistance is:
explanation: Maximum power transfer theorem: R_{L} = R_{th}.
why: At R_{th}/2 power is also 8/9 of maximum.
A short-circuit load receives zero power.

q: A source with V_{th} = 20 V and R_{th} = 5 Ω can deliver a maximum power of:
why: This is V²/R, power if R_{L} were a short across V_{th} with no R_{th}.

q: Efficiency of power transfer under maximum power transfer conditions is:
explanation: With R_{L} = R_{th}, equal power is dissipated in source and load, so η = 50%. That is why power systems are NOT operated at maximum power transfer.
why: That is neither source nor load share.

q: For maximum power transfer to an AC load, the load impedance must be:
options: The complex conjugate of the source impedance
explanation: Z_{L} = Z_{s}* cancels the reactance and matches resistance. (If only a resistive load is allowed, R_{L} = |Z_{s}|, which is a restricted case.)
why: Equal (not conjugate) impedance doubles the reactance.
This is the best case only when the load must be purely resistive.
A purely reactive load absorbs zero real power.

q: Superposition theorem cannot be used directly to find:
explanation: Power is proportional to I² — not linear — so powers from individual sources cannot be added. Find total current first, then P = I²R.
why: Capacitor voltage is a linear response.

q: While applying superposition, an ideal voltage source that is not acting is replaced by:
options: Its internal resistance in series with an open
explanation: Killing an ideal voltage source means making V = 0, i.e. a short circuit. Ideal current sources are replaced by open circuits. Dependent sources are left active.
why: Open circuit replaces a dead current source.
An ideal voltage source has zero internal resistance.

q: Superposition theorem is applicable only to circuits that are:
explanation: Superposition requires linearity (additivity and homogeneity). It works for AC, DC or mixed sources.
why: Linearity, not bilateral behaviour, is the requirement.
It also applies to AC and mixed-frequency sources.

q: Three equal resistors of 30 Ω each are connected in delta. The equivalent star resistance per arm is:
solution: For a balanced network R_{Y} = R_{Δ}/3
why: Delta and star values are not equal.

q: A delta has R_{ab} = 10 Ω, R_{bc} = 20 Ω, R_{ca} = 30 Ω. The equivalent star resistance connected to node a is:
why: Uses R_{ab}R_{bc}/60 for node a — wrong pair; that is R_{b}.
No valid product pair gives this (R_{b} = 3.33 Ω, R_{c} = 10 Ω).

q: Resistors of 4 Ω, 6 Ω and 10 Ω are in series across 40 V. The voltage across the 10 Ω resistor is:
why: The full supply is shared among three resistors.
That is the drop across the 4 Ω and 6 Ω together.

q: Equivalent resistance of 6 Ω and 3 Ω in parallel is:
why: Parallel value lies between 0 and the smaller resistor but is 2 Ω here.
Average of the two, not parallel.

q: A circuit has V_{th} = 10 V and R_{th} = 2 Ω. Its Norton equivalent is:
solution: R_{N} = R_{th} = 2 Ω, in parallel with the current source
explanation: R_{N} = R_{th} = 2 Ω, in parallel with the current source
why: Norton resistance is in parallel, not series.
R_{N} equals R_{th}, not its reciprocal.

q: RMS value of a sinusoidal voltage with peak 100 V is approximately:
Peak value of a 220 V (rms) household supply is about:
why: 380 V is roughly a 3-phase line voltage, not a peak.

q: Form factor of a pure sinusoidal wave is:
explanation: Form factor = rms/average = 0.707V_{m}/0.637V_{m} = 1.11. Peak (crest) factor = V_{m}/V_{rms} = 1.414.
why: Form factor of a square wave.

q: In a purely inductive AC circuit, current:
explanation: v = L di/dt, so current lags voltage by 90° (ELI: E before I in an inductor).
why: In phase only for a pure resistance.

q: In a purely capacitive circuit the average power consumed is:
explanation: Phase angle is 90°, so P = VI cos 90° = 0. Energy is stored and returned every half cycle.

q: Inductive reactance of a 0.1 H coil at 50 Hz is approximately:
why: That is πfL, missing the factor 2.

q: Capacitive reactance of a 100 µF capacitor at 50 Hz is approximately:
why: Off by a factor of 10 (C taken as 1000 µF).
Off by a factor of 10 (C taken as 10 µF).

q: At series resonance in an RLC circuit:
options: Impedance is maximum and current minimum
Impedance is minimum and current maximum
explanation: At resonance X_{L} = X_{C}, so Z = R (minimum), current = V/R (maximum) and power factor = 1.
why: Power factor is unity at resonance.
Current is in phase with voltage.

q: At resonance, an ideal parallel LC (tank) circuit draws a line current that is:
explanation: Inductor and capacitor branch currents are equal and opposite, so line current is minimum and impedance maximum (a rejector circuit).
why: The capacitor current circulates inside the tank and can be much larger than line current.
At resonance the small line current is in phase with voltage.

q: Resonant frequency of a series circuit with L = 10 mH and C = 10 µF is approximately:
A series RLC circuit has R = 10 Ω, L = 0.1 H, C = 10 µF. Its quality factor Q is:
why: 100 is √(L/C) only, before dividing by R.

q: Bandwidth of a series resonant circuit is related to its quality factor Q by:
explanation: BW = f_{0}/Q = R/(2πL). A higher Q gives a narrower bandwidth (more selective circuit).
why: Higher Q would then widen the band — opposite of reality.

q: A load takes 800 W at 1000 VA. Its reactive power is:
why: S − P is not valid; powers add as a triangle.

q: The power factor of a load with impedance Z = 3 + j4 Ω is:
explanation: +j means inductive, so lagging
why: +j4 is inductive, so the pf is lagging, not leading.
3/4 = R/X is not a power factor.

q: In a balanced star-connected system the line voltage is:
explanation: V_{L} = √3 V_{ph} and leads the phase voltage by 30°; I_{L} = I_{ph} in star.

q: In a balanced delta-connected load the line current is:
explanation: I_{L} = √3 I_{ph} in delta; V_{L} = V_{ph}.

q: A balanced 3-phase load draws 10 A at 400 V line and 0.8 pf. Active power is about:
Line voltage of a star-connected supply is 400 V. Phase voltage is about:
In the two-wattmeter method of measuring 3-phase power, one wattmeter reads zero when the power factor is:
why: At unity pf both read equal.
At 0.866 (φ = 30°) one reads twice the other.
At zero pf readings are equal and opposite.

q: In the two-wattmeter method W1 = 2 kW and W2 = 1 kW. The load power factor is about:
why: pf 0.5 would make one meter read zero.

q: In a balanced 3-phase, 4-wire star system the neutral current is:
explanation: Three equal currents 120° apart sum to zero, so the neutral carries no current (ignoring triplen harmonics).
why: Only triplen harmonic currents add in the neutral.
Only for an unbalanced or single-phase condition.

q: Time constant of an RC circuit with R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 µF is:
In one time constant, a charging capacitor reaches about what percentage of its final voltage?
explanation: v = V(1 − e^{−1}) = 0.632V. After 5τ it is effectively fully charged (99.3%).

q: Time constant of an RL circuit with L = 2 H and R = 4 Ω is:
Under DC steady-state conditions, an ideal inductor behaves as a(n):
options: Resistor equal to its reactance at 50 Hz
explanation: With constant current, di/dt = 0 so v = L di/dt = 0: a short circuit. A capacitor at DC steady state behaves as an open circuit.
why: A zero current source is an open circuit.
That is the capacitor at DC.

q: The SI unit of admittance is:
explanation: Admittance Y = 1/Z, measured in siemens (S), formerly mho.
why: Ohm is the unit of impedance.

q: The reciprocity theorem is applicable to:
options: Linear bilateral networks with a single source
explanation: Interchanging the positions of a single source and the response leaves the ratio unchanged — valid only for linear, bilateral, passive networks.
why: Non-linear networks do not obey it.

q: Tellegen's theorem is valid for:
options: Any lumped network obeying KCL and KVL
explanation: Tellegen's theorem (Σ v_{k}i_{k} = 0) depends only on network topology via KCL and KVL, so it holds for linear, non-linear, time-varying, active or passive lumped networks.
why: It holds for instantaneous values under any excitation.

q: A 24 V source with 6 Ω internal resistance feeds a 12 Ω resistor. Thevenin equivalent across the 12 Ω resistor is:
why: 8 V is the drop across the 6 Ω resistor.
Resistances are in parallel as seen from the terminals, not series.
Neither value follows from the divider.

q: In the circuit above (24 V, 6 Ω internal, 12 Ω across the terminals), the maximum power that a variable load across the 12 Ω can receive is:
Energy stored in a 0.5 H inductor carrying 4 A is:
why: Omits the ½ and uses I (0.5 × 4).

q: Energy stored in a 10 µF capacitor charged to 100 V is:
why: Omits the ½ and uses V instead of V² (CV).

q: v = 100 sin(314t + 30°) V and i = 10 sin(314t − 30°) A. Average power drawn is:
why: Uses peak values and no power factor.

q: The frequency of v = 325 sin(314t) V is:
explanation: = 50 Hz
why: 314 is the angular frequency in rad/s.

q: The internal resistance of an ideal current source is:
explanation: An ideal current source delivers the same current whatever the load, so its parallel internal resistance is infinite. An ideal voltage source has zero internal resistance.
why: That describes matching, not an ideal source.
Zero is an ideal voltage source.

q: Millman's theorem is used to:
options: Find the power factor of a load
Replace several parallel voltage sources (with series resistances) by one equivalent source
explanation: Millman: V_{eq} = Σ(V_{k}/R_{k}) / Σ(1/R_{k}) and R_{eq} = 1/Σ(1/R_{k}) for branches in parallel.
why: That is the maximum power transfer theorem.
Power factor is not its purpose.

q: Superposition theorem is based on the principle of:
explanation: Superposition requires additivity and homogeneity — the definition of a linear system.

q: A network made only of resistors, inductors and capacitors (no sources of energy) is called:
explanation: R, L and C cannot deliver net energy over time, so the network is passive.
why: Ideal R, L, C are linear.
Active networks contain energy sources (or transistors, op-amps).
R, L, C are bilateral elements.

q: Nodal analysis is based on:
explanation: Node equations sum currents at each node (KCL); mesh analysis uses KVL.
why: Ohm’s law is used inside the equations but the method rests on KCL.

q: A series RLC circuit operated below its resonant frequency behaves as:
explanation: Below f_{0}, X_{C} > X_{L}, so net reactance is capacitive and current leads. Above f_{0} it is inductive.

q: Two branches, each made of two 8 Ω resistors in series, are connected in parallel. Equivalent resistance is:
why: 4 Ω is two single 8 Ω resistors in parallel, not two 16 Ω branches.

q: A 230 V, 1 kW heater is operated at 115 V. Power consumed (resistance constant) is:
Power factor of a series circuit with R = 8 Ω and X_{L} = 6 Ω is:
explanation: inductive → lagging

q: The dual of a series RLC circuit driven by a voltage source is a:
options: Parallel RLC driven by a voltage source
Series RLC driven by a current source
Parallel GCL circuit driven by a current source
explanation: Duality swaps series↔parallel, voltage↔current, R↔G, L↔C, KVL↔KCL.

q: A coil draws 2 A from 100 V DC and 1 A from 100 V, 50 Hz AC. Its inductive reactance is about:
A wattmeter connected in an AC circuit reads:
explanation: It reads VI cos φ, the real power; a VAR-meter reads reactive power.
why: VA = V × I, read by voltmeter–ammeter.

q: A 20 V source feeds two 10 Ω resistors in series. Looking across the lower resistor, the Norton current is:
explanation: = 2 A (equivalently, short-circuit current = 20/10 = 2 A)
